LOS ANGELES, California (CNN) -- A former engineer for Rockwell International and Boeing was convicted Thursday of economic espionage and acting as an agent of China, authorities said. A Delta IV rocket launches on March 10, 2003 at Cape Canaveral, Florida. Dongfan "Greg" Chung, 73, was accused of stealing restricted technology and Boeing trade secrets, including information related to the space shuttle program and the Delta IV rocket. U.S. District Judge Cormac J. Carney convicted him on charges of conspiracy to commit economic espionage; six counts of economic espionage to benefit a foreign country; one count of acting as an agent of the People's Republic of China; and one count of making false statements to the FBI, according to a statement from federal prosecutors. Carney presided over Chung's three-week bench trial last month. In a bench trial, there is no jury and the judge decides whether to convict a defendant after hearing testimony. Chung was free on bond after his arrest by FBI agents and NASA investigators in February 2008. He was taken into custody after Carney's ruling was read. Chung, a native of China who is a naturalized United States citizen, was employed by Rockwell International from 1973 until Boeing acquired its defense and space unit in 1996, and by Boeing thereafter. He retired from Boeing in 2002, but returned as a contractor, a position he held until September 2006, prosecutors said. Chung held a "secret" security clearance, authorities said. "For years, Mr. Chung stole critical trade secrets from Boeing relating to the space shuttle and the Delta IV rocket -- all for the benefit of the government of China," said David Kris, assistant attorney general for national security, in the prosecutors' statement. "Today's verdict should serve as a warning to others willing to compromise America's economic and national security to assist foreign governments." The case against Chung resulted from an investigation into another engineer who obtained information for China. That engineer, Chi Mak, and several of his relatives were convicted of providing defense articles to the PRC, authorities said. Mak was sentenced to more than 24 years in prison last year. According to evidence presented at trial, individuals in the Chinese aviation industry began sending tasks to Chung via letter as early as 1979, federal prosecutors said. Over the years, the letters directed Chung to collect data related to the space shuttle and various military and civilian aircraft. In his letters back to China, Chung referenced materials he had already sent, including 24 manuals relating to the B-1 bomber, which Rockwell had forbidden for distribution outside the company and federal agencies. In addition, between 1985 and 2003, Chung traveled to China several times and met with government officials. His contacts in China discussed these trips in letters and recommended methods of passing information, authorities said. In a 2006 search of Chung's home, FBI and NASA agents found more than 250,000 pages of documents from Boeing, Rockwell and other defense contractors in the house and in its crawl space, prosecutors said. They included "scores of binders containing decades' worth of stress analysis reports, test results and design information for the space shuttle." Each economic espionage charge carries a maximum sentence of 15 years in prison and a $500,000 fine, authorities said. The charge of acting as an agent for a foreign government carries a maximum penalty of 10 years in prison and a $250,000 fine. The charges of conspiracy to commit economic espionage and making false statements to federal investigators each carry a maximum sentence of five years in prison and a $250,000 fine. Chung is set for sentencing November 9.

According to a statement released by federal prosecutors, U.S. District Judge Cormac J. Carney found Chung guilty on multiple counts: conspiracy to engage in economic espionage, six separate counts of economic espionage benefiting a foreign nation, acting on behalf of the People's Republic of China, and lying to FBI investigators.

Judge Carney oversaw the three-week trial without a jury last month—a format in which the presiding judge alone determines guilt after reviewing the evidence and testimony presented.

Following his February 2008 arrest by FBI and NASA investigators, Chung had remained free on bond until the judge's verdict was announced, at which point he was immediately taken into custody.

Born in China but later becoming a naturalized American citizen, Chung began working for Rockwell International in 1973. When Boeing purchased Rockwell's defense and space division in 1996, he continued his employment there. Although he officially retired from Boeing in 2002, he came back as a contractor and remained in that role until September 2006. During his career, he held a "secret" level security clearance, officials noted.

"For years, Mr. Chung stole critical trade secrets from Boeing relating to the space shuttle and the Delta IV rocket—all for the benefit of the government of China," stated David Kris, the assistant attorney general overseeing national security matters, in the official prosecution statement. He added that the verdict "should serve as a warning to others willing to compromise America's economic and national security to assist foreign governments."

This case emerged as a byproduct of a separate investigation targeting another engineer, Chi Mak, who had also been funneling information to China. Mak, along with several family members, was previously convicted of supplying defense-related materials to the PRC, with Mak receiving a sentence exceeding 24 years in prison last year.

Trial evidence showed that Chinese aviation industry contacts had been assigning tasks to Chung through written correspondence as far back as 1979, prosecutors said. These letters instructed him over the years to gather information concerning the space shuttle and multiple military and commercial aircraft programs.

Chung's return correspondence to China mentioned materials already transmitted, including two dozen technical manuals for the B-1 bomber—documents Rockwell had explicitly prohibited from being shared outside the company or government agencies.

Additionally, Chung made several trips to China between 1985 and 2003, during which he met with government officials there. His Chinese contacts referenced these visits in their letters and suggested various techniques for transferring information, according to authorities.

When FBI and NASA agents searched Chung's residence in 2006, they discovered over 250,000 pages of documents belonging to Boeing, Rockwell, and other defense industry contractors, stored throughout the house including its crawl space. Among these materials were numerous binders containing decades' worth of stress analysis reports, testing data, and design specifications for the space shuttle, prosecutors reported.

Under sentencing guidelines, each economic espionage count carries a potential 15-year prison term and up to $500,000 in fines. The charge of acting as a foreign agent could bring up to 10 years in prison and a $250,000 fine, while both the conspiracy charge and the false statements charge each carry maximum penalties of five years imprisonment and $250,000 in fines.

Chung's sentencing hearing has been scheduled for November 9.

Los Angeles is renowned for its incredible diversity. The city is home to people from virtually every corner of the globe, creating a vibrant tapestry of cultures, languages, and traditions. **By CNN Staff**

A federal jury has convicted a former aerospace engineer who worked for major U.S. defense contractors of conspiring to pass sensitive technical information to agents of the Chinese government over the course of several years, according to the Justice Department.

Prosecutors said the engineer, who held security clearances during a career spanning work with Boeing and Rockwell International, used his access to proprietary and export-controlled technical data to benefit Chinese state interests, in violation of U.S. export control laws and federal espionage statutes.

## The Case

According to court documents and evidence presented at trial, the engineer allegedly began cultivating relationships with individuals connected to Chinese aerospace and defense programs years before his arrest. Prosecutors argued he transmitted technical documents, engineering data, and other proprietary information related to U.S. aerospace and space systems — some of it tied to military and dual-use technology subject to strict export controls under the Arms Export Control Act and International Traffic in Arms Regulations (ITAR).

FBI agents testified that the investigation began after analysts flagged unusual travel patterns and financial transactions, which prompted a multi-year counterintelligence operation involving surveillance, forensic analysis of electronic devices, and cooperation from confidential sources.

"This conviction sends a clear message that the theft of American technology and trade secrets on behalf of foreign governments will not go unpunished," a Justice Department official said in a statement following the verdict.

## Defense Response

Defense attorneys maintained throughout the trial that their client was engaged in legitimate academic and professional exchanges common within the global aerospace industry, and that prosecutors overstated the sensitivity of the information involved. They argued the case relied heavily on circumstantial evidence and said they intend to appeal the verdict.

## Broader Context

The case is the latest in a string of prosecutions brought by the Justice Department's China Initiative and its successor efforts targeting economic espionage, as U.S. officials have grown increasingly concerned about the transfer of advanced aerospace, semiconductor, and defense-related technology to Beijing.

FBI Director Christopher Wray has repeatedly warned that Chinese intelligence services aggressively target current and former U.S. defense industry employees, often through front companies, academic partnerships, and recruitment at international conferences.

Boeing and Rockwell, now part of Rockwell Collins/Collins Aerospace under RTX Corporation, both said in statements that they cooperated fully with federal investigators and have robust internal security protocols to prevent unauthorized disclosure of sensitive data.

## What's Next

The engineer faces a sentencing hearing in the coming months, where he could face decades in federal prison depending on the specific charges of conviction, which reportedly include conspiracy to violate export control laws, economic espionage, and making false statements to federal investigators.

Legal experts say the case underscores the increasing scrutiny facing dual-national employees and contractors in the U.S. defense and aerospace sectors, as well as the tension between international scientific collaboration and national security enforcement.

Dongfan "Greg" Chung was a Chinese-born engineer who worked as a contractor for Rockwell International and later Boeing, primarily involved in aerospace projects including the Space Shuttle program and other defense/aviation technology.

Chung was investigated and prosecuted for stealing trade secrets and sensitive technical documents related to U.S. aerospace and defense programs, allegedly passing this information to China over several decades. In 2009, Chung was convicted of **economic espionage** and related charges, making him one of the first individuals convicted under the Economic Espionage Act of 1996 for spying on behalf of China. He was found guilty of six counts, including economic espionage, acting as an unregistered foreign agent, and conspiracy.

## Sentencing
Chung was sentenced to **15 years and 8 months in federal prison**. Given his age at sentencing (in his 70s), this amounted to what was effectively a life sentence. The case was notable for its severity, reflecting the scale and duration of the espionage activity, which prosecutors argued spanned decades.

## Connection to the Chi Mak Case
Chung's case is closely linked to that of **Chi Mak**, another engineer convicted in a related Chinese espionage scheme:

- Both cases emerged from overlapping FBI investigations into Chinese intelligence-gathering operations targeting U.S. defense contractors in California.
- Chi Mak, who worked for a defense contractor (Power Paragon), was convicted in 2007 for conspiracy to export U.S. defense technology to China.
- Evidence and leads from the Chi Mak investigation reportedly helped authorities uncover and build the case against Chung, as investigators found connections between the two men and their networks.
- Both cases were part of a broader pattern of concern about Chinese intelligence services recruiting or tasking engineers of Chinese descent working in sensitive U.S. defense and aerospace industries to systematically collect and transfer technical information over long periods.

Together, the Chung and Mak cases represented some of the most significant economic espionage prosecutions of that era, highlighting vulnerabilities in the U.S. defense industrial base to long-term intelligence collection efforts.

**Former Boeing Engineer Convicted of Stealing Space Shuttle, Rocket Secrets for China**

*By CNN Staff*

SANTA ANA, California (CNN) — A federal jury has found a former Boeing engineer guilty of economic espionage, convicting him of stealing sensitive aerospace technology — including data related to the space shuttle and the Delta IV rocket program — and passing it to China over the course of decades.

Dongfan "Greg" Chung, 73, a Chinese-American engineer who worked for Rockwell International and later Boeing, was convicted Thursday on charges under the Economic Espionage Act, along with related counts of acting as an agent of a foreign government and obstruction of justice. He now faces the possibility of decades in federal prison.

Prosecutors said Chung began funneling proprietary information to Chinese aviation officials as early as the 1970s and continued for more than 30 years, even after his formal retirement, when he returned to Boeing as a contractor.

**A Trove of Stolen Documents**

Federal investigators say they recovered roughly 300,000 pages of sensitive documents from Chung's California home during a 2006 search — material authorities allege included technical data on the space shuttle, the Delta IV rocket, and military aircraft such as the C-17 transport plane and the B-1 bomber.

"This was not a momentary lapse in judgment," a Justice Department spokesperson said following the verdict. "This was a calculated, sustained effort over multiple decades to provide critical U.S. aerospace technology to a foreign government."

Prosecutors also presented letters and travel records they said showed Chung had been in direct contact with Chinese government representatives, who allegedly requested specific categories of technical information related to U.S. space and defense programs.

**Defense Pushback**

Chung's defense attorneys argued that their client was a dedicated Boeing employee who kept extensive files as part of his meticulous engineering habits, not for the purpose of espionage. They contended prosecutors failed to prove any documents were transmitted directly to Chinese officials with the intent to harm the United States.

"Mr. Chung is an American citizen who spent his career working for U.S. companies," a defense attorney said outside the courthouse. "We believe the government's case relied heavily on inference rather than direct evidence of intent."

**Broader Concerns Over Espionage**

The case is one of several in recent years involving allegations that China has sought to acquire sensitive U.S. aerospace and defense technology through current or former employees at American contractors. U.S. officials have repeatedly warned that economic espionage tied to foreign governments poses a growing threat to national security.

"This verdict sends a clear message," the U.S. Attorney overseeing the case said in a statement. "Those who abuse positions of trust to steal American technology and hand it to a foreign power will be held accountable."

**Sentencing Ahead**

Chung is scheduled to be sentenced in the coming months. He faces a maximum sentence of life in prison on the economic espionage charges alone, though legal experts say federal sentencing guidelines will likely result in a term of years rather than a life sentence.

Boeing, in a brief statement, said it fully cooperated with federal investigators throughout the case and reiterated its commitment to protecting proprietary technology and complying with U.S. export control laws.

The case remains a focal point in the broader national conversation about safeguarding sensitive aerospace and defense technology from foreign intelligence efforts.

*CNN's coverage of this case is ongoing.*

# Former Boeing Engineer Convicted of Acting as Agent for China, Faces Decades in Prison

**SANTA ANA, Calif.** — A federal jury has convicted Dongfan "Greg" Chung, a former Boeing engineer, on multiple charges stemming from his decades-long effort to pass sensitive aerospace and defense information to the People's Republic of China, the Department of Justice announced today.

## The Verdict

Chung, 73, a naturalized U.S. citizen born in China, was found guilty on charges including acting as an illegal agent of the People's Republic of China, conspiracy, and making false statements to the FBI. The conviction caps a lengthy investigation into what prosecutors describe as one of the longest-running cases of economic espionage conducted on behalf of a foreign government in U.S. history.

Prosecutors presented evidence that Chung, who worked as a stress analyst for Boeing and its predecessor companies for over three decades, retained and passed sensitive documents related to the Space Shuttle program, the Delta IV rocket, and military aircraft including the C-17 transport plane, to Chinese aviation officials over a period spanning from the 1970s through the mid-2000s.

## Statements from Officials

Officials from the Department of Justice and the FBI emphasized the significance of the verdict in the broader context of national security enforcement.

A senior DOJ national security official stated:

> "This conviction sends an unmistakable message that those who betray the trust placed in them by American companies—and by extension, the American people—by stealing sensitive technology for a foreign power will be held accountable. Mr. Chung spent decades systematically undermining the security interests of the United States, and today's verdict reflects the seriousness with which we pursue these threats."

An FBI official involved in the investigation added:

> "This case illustrates the patient, long-term nature of economic espionage threats facing our country. Mr. Chung was not a spy in the traditional sense of dead drops and disguises—he was a trusted employee who methodically collected and retained protected information over the course of his career, motivated by loyalty to a foreign government rather than the country that had given him citizenship and employment."

Prosecutors also noted that the case relied heavily on physical evidence recovered from Chung's residence, including handwritten notes, diaries, and documents that detailed his communications with Chinese officials and outlined tasking he had received to acquire specific categories of technical information.

## Details of the Scheme

A federal jury has convicted a former aerospace engineer on charges of economic espionage and theft of trade secrets after a multi-year FBI investigation revealed he had transferred sensitive defense technology data to a foreign government, according to Department of Justice officials.

## The Investigation

The FBI's investigation began after the engineer's employer, a major U.S. defense contractor, flagged unusual data access patterns on internal servers containing information related to classified propulsion and guidance systems used in military aircraft.
